en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
14. The Exposition of the Questions of the Young Man Posāla:
"He who points out the past," [said the Venerable Posāla].
Unshaken, with doubts severed,
you have reached the further shore of all phenomena;
I have come to you with a question.
"He who declares the past":
"He" refers to the Blessed One, the Self-Existent One.
Without a teacher, he himself fully awakened to the truths regarding phenomena unheard of before; therein he attained omniscience and mastery over the powers (*bala*).
"He reveals the past," thus he is called the Blessed One; for the Blessed One reveals his own past as well as that of others, he reveals the future, and he reveals the present.
How does the Blessed One reveal his own past?
The Blessed One reveals even one birth of his own past, he reveals two births, he reveals three births... [and so on].

He recollects; he recollects four births, he recollects five births, he recollects ten births, he recollects twenty births, he recollects thirty births, he recollects forty births, he recollects fifty births, he recollects a hundred births... [and so on].
Even a thousand births...
even a hundred thousand births...
even many aeons of world-dissolution...
He recollects many aeons of dissolution, many aeons of evolution, and many aeons of both dissolution and evolution:

"In such a place I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experience of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared in another place."
"There I was, with such a name, such a clan, such an appearance, such food, such experiences of pleasure and pain, and such a limit to my lifespan; passing away from there, I reappeared here.
Thus he declares his manifold past lives in their various aspects and details.
In this way, the Blessed One declares his own past.
How does the Blessed One declare the past of others?
The Blessed One declares one birth of others in the past; he declares two births; ... pe ...
he declares many eons of world-dissolution and evolution.

“In that place you were so named, of such a clan, of such an appearance, with such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a limit to your lifespan; passing away from there, you arose elsewhere.
There too you were so named, of such a clan, of such an appearance, with such food, experiencing such pleasure and pain, with such a limit to your lifespan; passing away from there, you arose here.
Thus he recollects his manifold past abodes with their modes and details.
In this way, the Blessed One declares the past of others.
When the Blessed One speaks the five hundred Jātaka tales, he declares the past of both himself and others;
when he speaks the Mahāpadāna Sutta, he declares the past of both himself and others; when he speaks the Mahāsudassana Sutta, he [declares the past of both himself and others].
He declares the past of both himself and others: while speaking the Mahāgovinda Sutta, he declares the past of both himself and others;
while speaking the Maghadevīya Sutta, he declares the past of both himself and others.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“Cunda, regarding the past, the Tathāgata possesses knowledge that follows after his mindfulness.
To whatever extent he wishes, to that extent he recollects.
And regarding the future, Cunda … [as before] …”
"But regarding the present time, Cunda, knowledge born of enlightenment arises in the Tathāgata thus:
'This is the final birth; now there is no further existence.
Knowledge of the degrees of the faculties of beings is a power of the Tathāgata; knowledge of the inclinations and underlying tendencies of beings [is a power of the Tathāgata].
The Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata is the knowledge of the Twin Miracle; the Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata is the knowledge of the attainment of great compassion;
the Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata is the knowledge of omniscience; the Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata is the knowledge free from obscurations;
the Tathāgata’s power of a Tathāgata is the unobstructed knowledge that is everywhere unattached and unimpeded.

Thus the Blessed One indicates his own past and that of others, indicates the future and the present; he declares, teaches, proclaims, establishes, reveals, analyzes, clarifies, and makes manifest. Thus it is said:
"He who indicates the past.
And so, the Venerable Posāla [said].
“Iccā” is a phonetic conjunction …pe… “Āyasmā” is a term of endearment …pe… “Posālo” is the name of that brahmin …pe… “Abhilāpo” means speech.
Thus spoke the Venerable Posāla.
"The one who is passionless and has severed doubt": here "passion" (ejā) is said to be craving (taṇhā).
It is lust, infatuation... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness.

That agitation, that craving, has been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One; it has been cut off at the root, made like a palm stump, rendered non-existent, and is subject to non-arising in the future.
Therefore, the Buddha is unagitated.
Because agitation has been abandoned, he is unagitated.
The Blessed One does not waver even at gain...
[and so on] ...he does not waver, does not shake, does not tremble, does not quiver, does not quake even at suffering; thus he is "unshaken.
"One whose doubts are severed": doubt is said to be *vicikicchā* (perplexity).
Doubt regarding suffering... [and so on] ...the trepidation of the mind, the mental distress—that uncertainty has been abandoned by the Buddha, the Blessed One;
it is cut off, severed, completely uprooted, stilled, relinquished, and calmed; it is incapable of arising again, burnt away by the fire of knowledge.
Therefore, the Buddha is one whose doubts are cut off.

“Unshaken, with doubts cut away, one who has gone beyond all phenomena”—thus said the Blessed One. He who has gone beyond all phenomena is one who has gone beyond through direct knowledge, gone beyond through full understanding, gone beyond through abandoning, gone beyond through development, gone beyond through realization, gone beyond through attainment, and gone beyond through direct knowledge of all phenomena...
[and so on] ...for him there is no further becoming in the cycle of birth and death.
One who has gone to the further shore of all phenomena.
I have come with a question; seeking the meaning through a question, I have come.
… “This will be a heavy burden for you,” [he said].
"I have come with a question.
Therefore, that brahmin said:
"He who points out the past..."
(Thus spoke the Venerable Posāla:
"Unshaken, with doubts severed,
he has gone beyond all phenomena."
"I have come with a question.
[The Buddha replied: "For one who has dispelled the perception of form and has abandoned the entire body..."
To one who sees that there is nothing whatsoever, both internally and externally—
I ask you, Sakka, about this knowledge.
How is such a person one who is to be led?
Regarding the phrase "one who has discarded the perception of form": what is the perception of form?

It is the perception, the act of perceiving, and the state of having perceived, belonging to one who has attained a fine-material-sphere absorption (rūpāvacara-samāpatti), or one who has been reborn there, or one who dwells in happiness in this very life.
This is the perception of form.

"One who has eliminated the perception of form" means that for one who has attained the four formless attainments, the perception of form has become eliminated, departed, transcended, surpassed, and passed beyond— thus,
"one who has eliminated the perception of form."

"Sabba-kāya-ppahāyino" means: his entire rebirth-body of form has been abandoned; through the transcendence of that factor and by way of suppression-abandonment, his body of form is abandoned—thus they are "those who have abandoned the entire body.
"And internally and externally, he sees that 'there is nothing at all.'"
"There is nothing whatsoever" is the attainment of the base of nothingness.
For what reason?
Because "there is nothing whatsoever" is the attainment of the base of nothingness.

When one mindfully enters the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, and having emerged from it, one causes that very consciousness to be unmade, made to disappear, and made to vanish, seeing "there is nothing whatsoever"—
for that reason it is called the attainment of the base of nothingness,
because one sees that there is nothing whatsoever both internally and externally.
"I ask Sakka about knowledge.
"Sakka" means Sakka.
The Blessed One is called Sakka because he went forth from the Sakyan clan... [and so on] ...he is also called Sakka because he has abandoned fear and terror and is free from horripilation.
“I ask about the knowledge of Sakka”: I ask about his knowledge, I ask about his wisdom, I ask about the Fully Awakened One.
“What kind of knowledge is to be desired? Of what nature, of what character, of what appearance, and of what likeness is it?”—thus [he asks].
I ask about knowledge regarding the Sakyans:
How is one of such a kind to be led? How is he to be guided, trained, conciliated, made wise, made to reflect, looked upon, and inspired with confidence?
How is higher knowledge to be generated by him?
“Of such a kind” means: of such a kind, of that sort, established in that, of that type, of that appearance—he who is the attainer of the attainment of the base of nothingness.
How is one of such a kind to be known?
Therefore, that brahmin said:
“For one who has overcome the perception of form,
who has abandoned the entire body,
both internally and externally...”
"To one who sees 'there is nothing at all,' I ask about his knowledge:
how is such a person to be understood?"
"O Posāla," said the Blessed One, "the Tathāgata has directly known all the stations of consciousness."
"He knows him as he stands, one liberated with that as his final resort.

The Blessed One knows all the stations of consciousness (viññāṇaṭṭhitiyo) by way of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) as four stations of consciousness; he knows them by way of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) as seven stations of consciousness.
How does the Blessed One know the four stations of consciousness by way of volitional formation?
For this was said by the Blessed One:

“Bhikkhus, when consciousness stands supported by form, it might persist; with form as its object, form as its foundation, and being moistened by delight, it would come to growth, increase, and abundance.”
“Or, bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist by depending on feeling...
or, bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist by depending on perception...

or, bhikkhus, if consciousness were to persist by depending on volitional formations, having volitional formations as its object and established upon volitional formations, it would attain growth, increase, and abundance through the addition of delight.”
In this way, the Blessed One knows the four stations of consciousness by way of volitional formations (*abhisaṅkhāra*).
How does the Blessed One know the seven stations of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*)?
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“There are, bhikkhus, beings who are diverse in body and diverse in perception—
such as humans, some devas, and some beings in the states of deprivation.
This is the first station of consciousness.”
"There are, bhikkhus, beings who are diverse in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of the Brahma-order who have first reappeared there.
This is the second station of consciousness.
There are, bhikkhus, beings who are uniform in body and diverse in perception, such as the Ābhassara gods."
This is the third station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings who are uniform in body and uniform in perception, such as the gods of Refulgent Glory (Subhakiṇha).
This is the fourth station of consciousness.

“There are, bhikkhus, beings who, with the complete surmounting of perceptions of form, with the passing away of perceptions of sensory impingement, and with non-attention to perceptions of diversity, [perceiving] ‘space is infinite,’ have reached the base of infinite space.
This is the fifth station of consciousness.
There are, bhikkhus, beings who, by completely surmounting the base of infinite space, [perceiving] ‘consciousness is infinite,’ have reached the base of infinite consciousness.”
This is the sixth station of consciousness.
There are, monks, beings who, having completely transcended the base of infinite consciousness, thinking "there is nothing," have reached the base of nothingness.
This is the seventh station of consciousness.
Thus the Blessed One knows all the stations of consciousness by way of rebirth-linking;
thus he is called "Posāla" by the Blessed One.
"Posāla," said the Blessed One, addressing that brahmin by name.
"Bhagavā" is a term of reverence... [as above] ...it is a designation based on realization, namely "Bhagavā"—thus, "Posāla," said the Blessed One.
"‘The Tathāgata is one who fully knows’:
the Tathāgata is one who fully knows, who understands, who discerns, who penetrates, and who pierces through.
For this was said by the Blessed One:"
“Cunda, even if something concerning the past is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare it.
Cunda, even if something concerning the past is true and correct but unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare that either.
But if something concerning the past is true, correct, and beneficial, the Tathāgata knows the proper time for declaring that very question.”
If, Cunda, it concerns the future...
or if, Cunda, it concerns the present, and it is untrue, incorrect, and unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare it.
Even if, Cunda, it concerns the present, and it is true and correct, but unbeneficial, the Tathāgata does not declare that either.
And if, Cunda, there is something present that is real, true, and beneficial, the Tathāgata knows the right time to provide an explanation for that question.
Thus, Cunda, regarding phenomena of the past, future, and present, the Tathāgata speaks at the proper time, speaks what is real, speaks what is beneficial, speaks on the Dhamma, speaks on the Vinaya;
therefore he is called the “Tathāgata.”

Whatever, Cunda, has been seen, heard, sensed, cognized, attained, sought after, or investigated by the mind in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans—
all that has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata.
Therefore, he is called the "Tathāgata.

And, Cunda, whatever the Tathāgata speaks, utters, or explains in the interval between the night he awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment and the night he passes away into the Nibbāna-element without remainder— [all that is true].
All that is exactly so and not otherwise.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.
Cunda, the Tathāgata acts in accordance with what he teaches; he acts as he speaks.
As he acts, so he speaks;
thus, as he speaks, so he acts, and as he acts, so he speaks.
Therefore, he is called the “Tathāgata.”

“Cunda, in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the conqueror, the unconquered, the all-seeing, the wielder of power.
Therefore he is called ‘Tathāgata’”—
thus the Tathāgata knows through direct realization.
“He knows him as he stands” means that the Blessed One knows the very matter here [in this life] by way of the volitional formations of kamma:
“This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, hell.
The Blessed One knows the very matter here by way of the volitional formations of kamma.
“This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the animal realm.
Thus the Blessed One knows this very matter here:
“This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will be reborn in the sphere of hungry ghosts,” by way of the formative force of kamma.
The Blessed One knows this very matter here and now by way of the formative activity of karma:
"This person, with the breakup of the body, after death, will arise among human beings.
The Blessed One knows this very matter here and now by way of the formative activity of karma: [and so forth].
“This person has practiced well; with the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a good destination, in a heavenly world.
For this was said by the Blessed One:
“In this case, Sāriputta, having encompassed another person’s mind with my own mind, I understand him thus:”

‘This person has practiced in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell.
But here, Sāriputta, having encompassed another person’s mind with my own mind, I understand:
‘This person has practiced in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in the animal realm.’
"Furthermore, Sāriputta, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus:

‘This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path, that with the breakup of the body, after death, he will be reborn in the realm of hungry ghosts.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus—"

‘This person has practiced in such a way, conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear among human beings. Furthermore, Sāriputta,
here I understand by encompassing his mind with my own that a certain person has practiced in such a way,
conducts himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path that, with the breakup of the body, after death, he will reappear in a happy destination, in a heavenly world.
Furthermore, Sāriputta, here I understand a certain person by encompassing his mind with my own mind thus:
"This person is practicing in such a way, conducting himself in such a way, and has entered upon such a path, that by the destruction of the taints,
he will realize for himself with direct knowledge in this very life the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom."
"Having attained, he dwells"—
thus one knows him as he stands:
"He is resolved upon that, that is his supreme goal."
“Resolved on the base of nothingness” means the base of nothingness.
“Resolved on” means resolved by way of liberation; resolved upon that, intent upon that, dominated by that.
Alternatively, the Blessed One knows: [that it is resolved upon that].
“This person is intent upon forms, intent upon sounds, intent upon odors, intent upon tastes,
intent upon tangibles, intent upon clans, intent upon assemblies, intent upon dwellings, intent upon gains, intent upon fame, intent upon praise,
intent upon pleasure, intent upon robes, intent upon almsfood, intent upon lodgings, and intent upon medicinal requisites for the sick.”

One devoted to the Suttantas; one devoted to the Vinaya; one devoted to the Abhidhamma; one devoted to the forest-dweller’s practice; one devoted to the alms-food-eater’s practice; one devoted to the refuse-rag-wearer’s practice;
one devoted to the three-robe-wearer’s practice; one devoted to the house-to-house-seeker’s practice; one devoted to the practice of not accepting food after the proper time;
one devoted to the sitter’s practice; one devoted to the practice of accepting whatever seat is offered; one devoted to the first jhāna; one devoted to the second jhāna.

"Intent on the third jhāna, intent on the fourth jhāna, intent on the attainment of the base of infinite space, intent on the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, intent on the attainment of the base of nothingness, intent on the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"—thus it is "intent.

"Having that as its ultimate resort" means having the base of nothingness as its ultimate resort; having karma as its ultimate resort, having fruition as its ultimate resort, heavy with karma, heavy with rebirth-linking.
Or else the Blessed One knows:
"This person has form as his ultimate goal... [and so on] ...he has the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as his ultimate goal."
with consciousness as their resort and with that as their final goal.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“All stations of consciousness...”
"Posāla," said the Blessed One,
"the Tathāgata knows this by direct knowledge;
he knows it as it stands."
"Whose final resort is wisdom.
Having understood the origin of nothingness,
[one knows] the fetter of delight.
Having directly known this thus,
one then sees it with insight there;
this is his knowledge of reality.
"For the brahmin who has lived the holy life.

Regarding "having known the source of nothingness": the "source of nothingness" refers to the formative volitional action (*kamma-abhisaṅkhāra*) that leads to the base of nothingness (*ākiñcaññāyatana*).
Having known that the formative volitional action leading to the base of nothingness is the "source of nothingness," [he knows] "clinging."
Having known, having known it as a bond, having known it as an impediment—having understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest—it is said:
"having known the origin of nothingness.
"The fetter of delight" means the fetter of delight is called formless lust (*arūparāga*).
Having known that action as stuck, adhered, and obstructed by formless lust; having known it as formless lust, as the fetter of delight;
having known it as a sticking, a binding, and an obstruction; and having thus understood, weighed, scrutinized, and analyzed it, he has made it manifest.
"‘Iti’ means the conjunction of words, the meeting of words, the completion of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequence of words; this is ‘iti.
‘The fetter of delight (nandisaṁyojana)’ is ‘iti.
‘Having thus directly known this’ means having thus directly known, understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified it."
Having thus directly known this, one then sees with insight therein. "Therein" means:

having entered the base of nothingness and emerged from it, one sees with insight those mental states and mental factors arisen therein as impermanent, one sees them as suffering, one sees them as a disease... [and so on].
"He sees, beholds, looks upon, contemplates, and examines [them] by way of escape"—
thus, "he sees with insight therein.
"This knowledge is true for him"— this knowledge is real, factual, as-it-is, and non-perverted for him.
This is the true knowledge of that brahmin who has lived the holy life. As for the term "brahmin":
he is called a brahmin because he has banished (bāhitattā) the seven [unwholesome] qualities... [as it is said: "Unattached and poised, he is called a Brahman."

"Of the Brahmin who has lived the holy life": starting from the virtuous worldling, the seven types of trainees dwell, live together, abide, and remain apart for the sake of attaining what has not been attained, for the sake of reaching what has not been reached, and for the sake of realizing what has not been realized.

The Arahant has lived the holy life; he has done what was to be done, laid down the burden, achieved his own goal, utterly destroyed the fetters of existence, and is completely liberated through final knowledge.
He has completed the residence, fulfilled the course of conduct... [and so on] ...the cycle of birth and death.
"There is no further becoming for that brahmin who has lived the holy life.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having understood that which arises from nothingness,
and [that it is] the fetter of delight;
having thus directly known this— ”
Then he sees with insight therein;
this is the true knowledge of that brahmin who has lived the holy life.
At the conclusion of the verse... [as before] ...
"Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am his disciple.
This is the fourteenth exposition: The Question of the Young Man Posāla.
